papers.title: Roost: Avian Influenza Host Genomics Resource
papers.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) causes mass mortality in poultry and wildlife, and puts already threatened species at further risk. Understanding differences in host susceptibility requires evidence currently scattered across publications, surveillance reports and genomic resources. We present Roost, a web resource that brings together more than 1,300 publications and reports, surveillance detections, and a catalogue of over 2,000 avian genome assemblies. Large language model-assisted literature analysis and comparative genomics link species, genes and molecular mechanisms to their supporting evidence. Around 51% of species with HPAI detections are not represented in the analysed corpus. Research concentrates on poultry, model organisms, and a small set of immune pathways. Research tracks neither mortality magnitude nor extinction risk; species with the largest recorded die-offs and threatened hosts alike remain largely unstudied. Roost makes this evidence, along with genome analyses, accessible to researchers and conservation practitioners, connecting documented disease with host biology and highlighting priorities for sequencing and functional research. Roost is available at http://josephguhlin.com/Roost

papers.title: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Reveals Distinct Cellular and Molecular Features of Steroid-Induced Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head Compared to Alcohol-Induced Osteonecrosis and Hip Osteoarthritis
papers.abstract: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) remains a devastating complication of glucocorticoid therapy and alcohol abuse, yet the pathophysiology is poorly understood. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed femoral head specimens from patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty due to steroid-induced ONFH, alcohol-induced ONFH, or hip osteoarthritis (OA). Our comprehensive analysis across conditions revealed etiology-specific cellular compositions and transcriptional profiles. Steroid-induced ONFH demonstrated a distinctive immunological signature characterized by a neutrophil-predominant, elevated innate-to-adaptive immune cell ratio compared to alcohol-induced ONFH or OA. T cell analysis revealed impaired maturation in steroid-induced ONFH, with abundant naive T cells but reduced mature CD4+ T cells and CD4+ memory T cells compared to both alcohol-induced ONFH and OA. In addition, compared to alcohol-induced ONFH, steroid-induced ONFH was associated with an increase in exhausted/dysfunctional CD8+ T cells which suggests an impaired response to stress and reflects chronic immune dysfunction. Within stromal cell populations, steroid-induced ONFH demonstrated an increase in pericytes, endothelial cells, and mesenchymal cell with osteogenic features as compared to both alcohol-induced ONFH or OA. These findings collectively reveal novel cellular mechanisms underlying steroid-induced ONFH which may contribute to further investigation of etiology-specific pathogenesis and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Cross-species epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity: Insights from Jonathan the Giant Tortoise and human centenarians
papers.abstract: Can epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity transcend species boundaries? By comparing findings from a previously published epigenomic study of Jonathan, a 194-year-old giant tortoise, based on buccal scrape and saliva samples, with the analyses of publicly available DNA methylation data from exceptionally long-lived humans based on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), this comparative study reveals intriguing molecular parallels across evolutionarily distant species. Human individuals aged 110+ years exhibited significantly higher global methylation entropy than those aged 60-82 years. Furthermore, 12 candidate genes displayed a distinctive promoter methylation entropy profile, with lower values at the youngest and oldest ages than in intermediate-age groups. Strikingly, these genes were enriched in telomere-related biological processes, highlighting a compelling link between epigenomic patterns and pathways implicated in aging. The correspondence between the findings in humans and previously reported observations in Jonathan suggests testable hypotheses about epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity that may be conserved across species and extend beyond tissue-specific effects.

papers.title: Comparative molecular analysis of histopathologic subtypes reveals shared epithelial remodeling yet distinct fibroblast programs in scleroderma lung disease
papers.abstract: Rationale: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) drives mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc), with a subset developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) resembling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite recognition of two distinct histopathologic patterns, the cellular basis of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) remains poorly understood. Objectives: To define shared and distinct cellular and molecular features of SSc-NSIP and SSc-UIP compared to IPF. Methods: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were performed on explanted lungs from patients with SSc-NSIP (n=6), SSc-UIP (n=6), or IPF (n=6), and control donors (n=12) with immunohistochemistry and western blot validation. Main Results: Across 120,254 nuclei from 35 cell types, there was striking similarity across fibrotic subgroups in epithelial, endothelial, and immune compartments, including alveolar type 1 cell loss, pathologic alveolar type 2 (AT2) gene expression, and expansion of COL15A1 endothelial cells and profibrotic macrophages. Diseased AT2s showed activation of the p53/DNA damage pathway. Aberrant basaloid (AB) cells were present in both SSc-ILD subtypes and transcriptionally similar to IPF ABs. They consistently neighbored profibrotic CTHRC1 fibroblasts, even in SSc-NSIP, despite lacking fibroblast foci. Fibroblast heterogeneity differentiated the histopathologic subtypes. Inflammatory fibroblasts were enriched in SSc-NSIP and CTHRC1 fibroblasts in UIP. AB-to-pathologic fibroblast crosstalk was defined by profibrotic signaling, with amplified TGF-{beta} signaling in UIP. Conclusions: Convergent epithelial remodeling is a hallmark of PPF in SSc-ILD and IPF. Fibroblast heterogeneity characterized by altered TGF-beta signaling distinguishes SSc-NSIP from SSc-UIP and IPF. Accelerated aging, DNA damage, and p53-dependent senescence pathways may represent shared drivers of PPF.

papers.title: GPBench: A benchmark framework for genomic prediction
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) has emerged as a powerful data mining strategy for disease risk assessment and molecular breeding. GP leverages genome-wide genetic variations and phenotypic information through a computational model to estimate genetic potential or disease risk. However, the field of GP still faces several major challenges: (i) dataset bias and insufficient representativeness; (ii) the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and a systematic benchmarking framework; (iii) heavy reliance on empirical expertise for experimental result interpretation, which hinders large-scale and systematic analysis. These issues make it difficult to conduct systematic cross-species evaluation and comparison of GP methods, and their authentic applications. To address these challenges, we established a standardized and extensible GP benchmark framework-GPBench. We first collected and harmonized public datasets from 16 species, covering animals, plants, and microorganisms, comprising 57 traits, 40,821 samples, and 493,821 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Then, using the standardized datasets, the framework evaluates 21 GP models and provides a unified assessment across four dimensions: effectiveness, sensitivity, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, we developed a large language model-based intelligent analysis system to facilitate the interpretation of GP experiments and model recommendations. GPBench provides the community with a fair, unified, and scalable platform (https://www.sdu-idea.cn/GPBench/) and an open-source library for comparing and optimizing GP methods, ultimately accelerating the application of GP in life sciences and biomedical research.

papers.title: Chromosome folding encodes mechanisms of cohesion maintenance
papers.abstract: After DNA replication, sister chromatids are physically linked by the cohesin complex. These cohesin linkages must be maintained for many hours for faithful chromosome segregation and DNA repair. Cohesin interacts with multiple rapidly exchanging cofactors, including SORORIN, which is often described as a molecular lock for cohesin on chromatin. How such transient SORORIN binding can protect cohesin over much longer timescales remains mechanistically unclear. Furthermore, how loop-extruding cohesins interact with and influence the positioning of sister-linking cohesins remains largely unknown. Here we show that changes in sister chromatid folding over time and after perturbations encode distinct signatures of the underlying mechanisms of cohesion maintenance. By integrating biochemical kinetics with polymer modeling, we infer cohesin turnover, motion, and encounter rules from these folding signatures. Repeated transient sequestration by SORORIN enables long-lasting protection yet acts as a quantitative modulator, rather than a binary switch for cohesion maintenance. Prolonging cohesin residence time by WAPL depletion exposes additional mechanisms shaping sister chromatid conformation, including pushing of sister-linking cohesins and diffusion of loop-extruding cohesins. Together, these results reveal how transient cofactor interactions regulate long-lived cohesin maintenance and establish sister chromosome organization as a quantitative readout of otherwise hidden molecular mechanisms.

papers.title: Synthetic MPRA perturbation supervision improves variant-effect prediction in sequence-to-function models
papers.abstract: Deep learning sequence-to-function (S2F) models learn to predict functional readouts, such as gene expression, from genetic sequence. However, these models are trained predominantly on the reference genome and struggle to accurately predict the effect of genetic variation on gene expression. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) explore the direct impact of genetic variation on gene expression, but saturation-mutagenesis MPRAs that measure variant effects directly remain limited, thereby restricting their use for fine-tuning S2F models. In this work, we investigate fine-tuning Borzoi, a state-of-the-art S2F model, on model-generated synthetic MPRA variant-effect data as a scalable alternative to overcome limits on the availability of supervised training data for genetic variation. First, we trained an ensemble of 16 models on 110,359 K562 MPRA measurements. Then, we distilled their predictions into a single student model using MPRA elements associated with 1,000 genes. The distilled model was subsequently used to generate synthetic variant-effect labels across increasing numbers of genes (50 to 1,000), with 600 variants per gene, to fine-tune Borzoi. Performance improved as we included more genes in training. In data-limited settings, training on more genes with fewer variants per gene performed better than training on fewer genes with more variants per gene, given the same number of total variants. Compared to pre-trained Borzoi, Borzoi fine-tuned on 600,000 synthetic samples across 1,000 genes increased Pearson correlation from 0.28 to 0.54 on CAGI5 promoter variants and from 0.39 to 0.46 on 903 GTEx fine-mapped whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs). Importantly, these improvements were achieved while preserving the pre-trained performance across all 7,611 output tracks. Furthermore, fine-tuned Borzoi recovered regulatory motifs identified by the MPRA model in genes unseen during training, suggesting that learned regulatory features can generalize across loci. Together, these results provide a proof of concept that model-generated synthetic supervision can improve variant effect prediction in S2F models while preserving their original pre-trained capabilities, offering a scalable strategy toward capturing the impact of genetic variation on gene regulation.

papers.title: A generative network model reveals hierarchical structural memory guiding post-mitotic 3D genome inheritance
papers.abstract: How three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is reestablished after mitosis to preserve gene regulatory programs and cell identity remains unresolved. We asked whether mitotic chromosome architecture contributes to cellular memory by preserving structural information while maintaining the flexibility required for cellular adaptation. Here we introduce HiCONA, a generative Bayesian framework that infers hierarchical genome organization and quantifies the structural contribution of individual interactions through an Entropy Impact Score. HiCONA resolves genome organization across multiple scales, revealing structure-defining interaction patterns underlying chromatin architecture, independently of experimental modality. We identify structurally impactful chromatin interactions retained during mitosis delineating distinct trajectories of post-mitotic genome reassembly. These mitotically preserved interactions are enriched for active, transcriptionally competent regulatory elements, consistent with a cis-encoded architectural memory subsequently remodeled by trans-acting regulators. Together, our findings suggest that molecular information retained on mitotic chromosomes guides structural trajectories, providing an architectural basis for epigenetic memory and post-mitotic genome inheritance.

papers.title: Ancient U/V sex chromosomes reveal slow expansion of recombination suppression in Polytrichaceae mosses.
papers.abstract: Sex chromosomes evolving in haploid versus diploid life cycles provide complementary systems for testing theories of sex chromosome evolution, yet haploid sex chromosomes remain poorly studied. In dioicous bryophytes, females and males carry non-recombining U and V chromosomes, respectively, providing a unique opportunity to examine the consequences of long-term recombination suppression independently of diploid heterogamety. Here, we characterize the U/V sex chromosomes of Polytrichaceae using chromosome-scale genomes from ten species. We identify homologous U/V chromosomes across the family and show that their non-recombining sex-determining regions (SDRs) originated early in Polytrichaceae evolution, approximately 124 million years ago. Despitetheir ancient origin, however, the SDRs have undergone limited expansion and are consistently flanked by large pseudoautosomal regions (PARs). The SDRs nevertheless show strong genomic signatures of recombination suppression, including reduced gene density, transposable-element accumulation, reduced diversity, high synonymous divergence, and altered codon usage. Yet they retain hundreds of genes and show limited evidence of functional degeneration. Their gene content is dynamic, with frequent lineage-specific gains and losses, while a conserved core of 60 orthogroups has persisted across all ten species for more than 100 million years. Comparisons across sex chromosome systems suggest that haploid U/V chromosomes retain more genes than similarly old diploid X/Y or Z/W chromosomes, consistent with a role for haploid selection in limiting degeneration. However, haploid selection alone cannot explain the limited SDR expansion observed in Polytrichaceae, suggesting that other factors also shape SDR evolution. Together, these results reveal an ancient U/V system in which recombination suppression has strong genomic consequences but has not driven extensive SDR expansion or functional degeneration. By decoupling recombination suppression from diploid heterogamety, U/V chromosomes provide a powerful framework for distinguishing the consequences of recombination arrest from those of ploidy in sex chromosome evolution.

papers.title: Local chromatin, 3D genome folding and transposon cargo shape Sleeping Beauty transposition
papers.abstract: The cut-and-paste DNA transposon Sleeping Beauty (SB) is widely used for genome engineering, mutagenesis and gene delivery. When mobilized from a genomic donor position ("launch site"), SB preferentially reintegrates locally (< 2 Mb), but factors governing its transposition from genomic sites remain incompletely understood. Here we analysed local transposition experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells to determine the influence of chromatin context and transposon cargo on SB transposition. Transposons in launch sites with transcriptionally active, accessible chromatin showed lower transposition efficiency. Large cargo and cargo with higher transcriptional activity also result in reduced transposition efficiency. After excision, local reintegration patterns closely resembled 3D contact frequencies of the launch site. This indicates that chromosome folding is a major determinant of the transposition pattern. Surprisingly, we did not detect any effect of the destination chromatin composition on reintegration efficiency. Cargo sequence modified the reintegration patterns: promoter-containing cargo increased both very proximal (<10kb) and interchromosomal transpositions, while CTCF binding sites in the cargo increased reintegration on the launch chromosome. Together, these results define key determinants of SB transposition in chromosomes and inform the design of SB-based genome engineering strategies.

papers.title: Urban enrichment of molestus ancestry and opposing temperature clines in a metropolitan Culex pipiens hybrid zone
papers.abstract: Hybridization between ecologically distinct lineages can fuel rapid adaptation when introgressed alleles are locally favored. The North American Culex pipiens assemblage, a principal West Nile virus vector east of the Mississippi, comprises three lineages---temperate Cx. pipiens f. pipiens, urban-specialist Cx. pipiens f. molestus, and subtropical Cx. quinquefasciatus---that meet in a mid-Atlantic hybrid zone where temperature and urbanization gradients intersect. Using whole-genome Pool-seq of 24 field populations and three lineage-reference pools across the Baltimore--Washington corridor, we find a weakly differentiated, Cx. pipiens f. pipiens-like background, richer in molestus- and quinquefasciatus-like ancestry toward the warmer end of the corridor. Urbanization impacts allele frequencies across the genome: molestus-like ancestry rises with impervious surface, independently of temperature and position, while Cx. quinquefasciatus-like ancestry does not. An 11.6 Mb chromosome 3 inversion is molestus-like in every population, most of all in urban ones, and tracks genome-wide molestus-like ancestry. Temperature acts locus by locus. On chromosome 1, a cluster of six CYP6 paralogs, a family implicated in insecticide resistance and thermal-stress response, shows rising Cx. quinquefasciatus-like ancestry and read depth with temperature. A chromosome 2 interval centered on a Yan ortholog, a repressor of cell differentiation, shows non-quinquefasciatus ancestry increasing with temperature, consistent with selection against Cx. quinquefasciatus-like introgression. Urban populations therefore carry more ancestry from the human-commensal lineage, while temperature moves ancestry both ways at individual loci. Both molestus and Cx. quinquefasciatus donors carry human-contact traits, so these patterns bear on how warming and urbanization will reshape arboviral risk.

papers.title: Transcriptional contingency in the early hematopoiesis of inherited bone marrow failure syndromes
papers.abstract: The inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS) are a group of heterogeneous genetic diseases caused by germline pathogenic variants in genes involved in hematopoiesis and genomic integrity. Despite sharing common phenotypical manifestations that have aided opportune diagnosis, such as bone marrow failure, congenital malformations and an increased predisposition to develop cancer, little is known about the shared and distinctive transcriptional programs in their hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells compartment that underlie the clinical manifestations of each disease. In this work we have successfully integrated and analyzed the publicly available scRNAseq datasets of HSPCs from patients with Fanconi anemia (FA) and Telomere Biology disorders (TBD), as well as healthy controls. Once integrated, we performed quality control metrics, as well as batch effect correction using different methods. Through dimensionality reduction, cell clustering and cell type annotation we found distinctive gene expression profiles per syndrome and per cell type, as well as orchestrated gene expression profiles, including upregulation of inflammatory pathways and cell proliferation pathways. This work shows the integration of datasets from FA and TBD, two major IBMFS, and provides the basis for an accumulative, comparative, and integrated atlas of scRNAseq data from patients with IBMFS.

papers.title: Shared and divergent features of the immune response to acute and chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection in mice revealed by cardiac transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Chagas disease is caused by infection with Trypanosoma cruzi and can result in chronic cardiomyopathy. However, the molecular programmes that define infected cardiac tissue, and how they change as the host-parasite relationship moves from acute pathogenic infection to long-term persistence, remain incompletely understood. Here, we used RNA sequencing to characterise host transcriptional responses in cardiac tissue during both acute and chronic infection in a mouse model. Cardiac parasite distribution was defined using bioluminescence imaging and histology, and RNA sequencing was performed on anatomically standardised cardiac tissue samples collected at both stages. Acute infection was associated with a broad interferon-driven immune activation, whereas during chronic infection this network contracted, with preservation of a tightly connected antigen presentation core centred on major histocompatibility complex genes and immunoproteasome components. Genes associated with extracellular matrix remodelling and fibrosis were not broadly activated. These findings indicate that reduced, but sustained immune activation, rather than widespread fibrotic transcriptional remodelling, represents a prominent feature of cardiac tissue in chronically infected mice. They identify a transition from an overtly inflammatory, pathogen-driven acute response to a more restricted chronic host-parasite equilibrium in which immune surveillance remains transcriptionally active despite very low and spatially intermittent cardiac infection. We identified a conserved 20-gene signature shared between acute and chronic stages. This overlap is consistent with continued or episodic parasite-derived stimulation and/or intrinsic host mechanisms that maintain cardiac immune surveillance. Thus, chronic T. cruzi infection can be viewed as a persistent host-parasite association in which biological coexistence does not imply benignity: immune containment and parasite persistence can occur alongside cumulative cardiac injury.

papers.title: Fentanyl and fentanyl-xylazine co-exposure influence mitochondrial transcriptional programs in human trophoblasts
papers.abstract: Introduction: Illicit fentanyl exposure during pregnancy is associated with adverse outcomes. Yet its direct effects and their underlying molecular mechanisms in human trophoblasts remain largely unknown. Xylazine and medetomidine, two [a]2-adrenergic agonists, were recently detected as adulterants in illicit fentanyl-containing products, and have been linked to worsened clinical outcomes. Methods: We assessed the transcriptional responses of human trophoblast stem (TS) cells in their cytotrophoblast state (TS-CTBs) and derived syncytiotrophoblasts (STBs) after 4-day and 9-day exposure to fentanyl alone or combined with medetomidine and xylazine (FMX). Results: Fentanyl alone produced modest gene expression changes in TS-CTBs, but consistently induced suppression of mitochondrial and ribosomal transcriptional programs in STBs regardless of exposure duration, an effect absent in parental TS-CTBs. 9-day FMX co-exposure influenced mitochondrial respiratory chain gene expression in derived STBs, resulting in discordant regulation of nuclear versus mitochondrial genome-encoded respiratory chain genes. Temporal pathway analysis reveals progressive trophoblast remodeling and dysregulation of mitochondrial transcriptional programs following fentanyl and FMX co-exposure. Discussion: Together, these findings illuminate trophoblast pathways affected by fentanyl alone and by FMX co-exposure, and establish a basis for future studies examining the functional and clinical relevance of these transcriptional responses.

papers.title: Quantifying heritability in functional regions of the coding and non-coding genome across diverse individuals
papers.abstract: Most heritability studies have focused on common genetic variation and have largely excluded non-European or highly admixed populations. Here, we estimated the whole-genome heritability (h2WGS) of seven complex traits using 73,600,953 autosomal and chromosome X variants for 198,931 unrelated individuals from three genetic similarity groups. Adjusting for population stratification, we showed that rare variants (minor allele frequency<0.01) explain 30.6-67.7% of h2WGS. We used simulations to show how functionally-stratified heritability can be inflated due to linkage with missing or lower-quality variants. Finally, after accounting for confounding effects, we found substantial heritability enrichment from variants in non-coding RNA exons (maximum fold enrichment, FE=8.7, P=3.56e-7), UTRs (23.0, P=3.46e-30), distal regulatory regions (33.8, P=3.26e-42), and protein-coding exons (58.0, P=7.78e-15). Our study provides a framework for investigating the genetic architecture of complex human phenotypes using diverse whole-genome sequencing data and highlights the contribution of rare and non-coding genetic variants to the heritability of complex traits.

papers.title: Comparative genomics of canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes across fungal plant pathogens: conserved siRNA-length windows define the scope for broad-spectrum spray-induced gene silencing
papers.abstract: Background. Spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS), in which double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) sprayed onto a crop is taken up by a fungal pathogen and silences an essential gene, is advancing as a biopesticide strategy. A recurring ambition is a broad-spectrum dsRNA: a single construct, directed at a conserved housekeeping gene, that controls several pathogens at once. Because silencing is driven by Dicer-processed small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) of roughly 21 nucleotides, the feasibility of this ambition depends on whether the target gene is conserved between pathogens at siRNA-length resolution, not merely at the level of overall gene identity. That resolution has not been mapped across the fungal plant-pathogen tree. Results. We screened eleven canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes of Fusarium graminearum (three CYP51 sterol 14-alpha-demethylases, six chitin synthases and two beta-tubulins) for perfect 21-nucleotide identity against the transcriptomes of twelve fungal plant pathogens spanning four taxonomic classes (Sordariomycetes, Leotiomycetes, Dothideomycetes and Basidiomycota). Of 27,116 candidate siRNA start positions across the eleven genes, only 2,108 (7.8%) were conserved as a perfect 21-mer in even one other pathogen, 148 in at least three, twelve in at least seven, and none in eight or more. Conservation decayed steeply with phylogenetic distance: the congeneric F. oxysporum shared 1,209 sites, other Sordariomycetes 262-313, Leotiomycetes and Dothideomycetes 62-204, Basidiomycota 41-48, and the reduced-genome obligate biotroph Blumeria graminis just one. The beta-tubulins carried the most broadly conserved individual sites (shared by up to seven pathogens), whereas CYP51C was the least conserved (shared by at most one). Even for the congener, perfect-match conservation covered only 4.5% of target positions and was concentrated in discrete windows rather than spread along the gene. Conclusions. At the siRNA-length resolution that governs silencing, perfect-match conservation of canonical antifungal targets is scarce and strongly clade-limited. A perfect-match broad-spectrum dsRNA is therefore realistic only within a narrow clade, in practice around the genus level; genus- and class-spanning broad-spectrum SIGS cannot rely on perfect siRNA identity and would require mismatch-tolerant design or pathogen-specific constructs. The conserved windows mapped here identify where clade-level broad-spectrum constructs can be placed, and the gene ranking (beta-tubulins most cross-targetable, CYP51C most pathogen-specific) provides a genome-guided basis for choosing antifungal dsRNA targets.

papers.title: Multi-modal in situ profiling of human cells using the AVITI24 platform characterizes single-cell responses to acute stress
papers.abstract: Cells begin to respond to stress within minutes, but how this early response depends on cell type, neighboring cells, or cell cycle phase has been difficult to determine, because bulk assays average across cells and synchronization can induce stress. We measured 338 transcripts, 48 proteins and phosphoproteins, and six cell paint stains in situ in 1.18 million single cells from four human cell lines exposed to H2O2, alone and in co-culture, and in A549 cells exposed to TNF-, cadmium, dithiothreitol or lipopolysaccharide. In A549 cells, five distinct stressors changed the same targets in the same direction within 15 min, differing mainly in magnitude, and modestly increased JNK phosphorylation. By 30 min of H2O2 treatment, immediate-early genes (FOS, JUN, DDIT3, DUSP1, NR4A1) were induced most strongly in HCT116 and A549 cells. These changes occurred across the whole cell population rather than in a responsive subset. Cell line-specific differences persisted in co-culture, and the response of MCF7 cells did not increase with the number of adjacent, strongly-responding A549 cells. Ordering cells along the cell cycle from the same measurements identified 106 cycle-associated transcripts, and the response varied more between cell lines than among cell cycle phases. Overall, the measured regulators respond to stress within 30 minutes through a largely shared program whose magnitude depends more on cell identity than on cell cycle state or neighboring cell type.

papers.title: A Chromosome Scale Genome Assembly for the Australian blue mussel Mytilus planulatus
papers.abstract: Mussels belonging to the genus Mytilus are among the world's most ecologically and economically important bivalve molluscs. Although the genus most likely originated in the Northern Hemisphere, the evolutionary history of Southern Hemisphere lineages, including the timing and number of colonisation events leading to the extant Australian populations, remains debated. Limited genomic resources have hindered the reconstruction of these evolutionary histories. In Australia, distinguishing native Mytilus planulatus from invasive Mytilus galloprovincialis is critical for biosecurity and conservation, but previous molecular approaches lacked sufficient resolution to resolve species boundaries and hybridisation patterns. Here, we present the first chromosome-scale reference genome for M. planulatus. The assembly consists of 14 chromosomes and over 51,000 annotated protein-coding genes per haplotype. Comparative analysis revealed extensive structural variation and widespread hemizygosity despite a largely conserved chromosomal organisation relative to M. galloprovincialis. Population analyses using SNPs and gene presence-absence variation in resequenced individuals confirmed previously inferred patterns of population structure and establish this reference genome as a valuable resource for future studies of genome evolution, adaptation and population genomics in Mytilus.

papers.title: Ultrasensitive detection of neuronal DNA using genome-wide non-CG methylation patterns
papers.abstract: Methylation-based liquid biopsies can identify the tissue origins of circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA). A major constraint on the sensitivity of these assays is the limited number of cell-type-specific CpG markers. Here we exploit the high abundance of non-CpG (CpH) methylation in neurons to enable ultrasensitive detection of neuronal DNA. We show that neurons carry 100-fold higher CpH methylation than other tissues, in which apparent CpH methylation largely reflects experimental artifacts. Using a computational criterion to identify cfDNA molecules carrying clusters of methylated CpA sites, we detect neuronal DNA at proportions as low as 20 parts per million. Analysis of 231 samples from 163 individuals revealed minimal neuronal cfDNA in the plasma of healthy subjects; elevated levels in patients with measles or acute neurological conditions; strikingly high levels in brain-dead donors, indicating extensive ongoing neuronal death; and the highest levels in the cerebrospinal fluid of patients in a neurological intensive care unit. These findings establish genome-wide, fragment-level analysis of non-CpG methylation as an ultrasensitive approach for blood-based monitoring of brain injury and disease.

papers.title: An Isogenic iPSC Model of LMNA p.R482W Recapitulates Adipocyte Dysfunction in Familial Partial Lipodystrophy Type 2
papers.abstract: Familial partial lipodystrophy type 2 (FPLD2) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in LMNA, most commonly p.R482W, and is characterized by selective loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue, severe insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia. The cellular mechanisms underlying adipocyte dysfunction in FPLD2 remain incompletely understood, in part because existing in vitro models rely on patient-derived, non-isogenic cell lines or require non- physiologic transgene overexpression to achieve adipogenic differentiation. Here, we describe a CRISPR/Cas9-edited isogenic iPSC model of FPLD2 in which the heterozygous LMNA c.1444C>T (p.R482W) variant was introduced into a healthy donor-derived iPSC line. Using a transgene-free mesenchymal progenitor differentiation protocol, we generated LMNAp.R482W and isogenic control adipocytes and characterized their transcriptomic and functional phenotypes. Bulk RNA- sequencing demonstrated strong concordance in adipogenesis gene expression between genotypes during differentiation (Pearson {rho} = 0.968), yet LMNAp.R482W adipocytes exhibited significant downregulation of key adipogenic, lipid-handling, and extracellular matrix genes compared to isogenic controls. Functionally, LMNAp.R482W adipocytes showed markedly impaired glucose uptake under both basal and insulin-stimulated conditions, consistent with severe insulin resistance. Seahorse extracellular flux analysis revealed a globally quiescent metabolic state with significantly reduced oxygen consumption rate (126.5 vs. 261.5 pmol/min, p < 0.0001) and extracellular acidification rate (27.6 vs. 46.7 mpH/min, p < 0.0001). To validate these findings in human tissue, gene set enrichment analysis results from the iPSC model were compared to single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from subcutaneous white adipose tissue biopsies of individuals with FPLD2 carrying the LMNA p.R482W variant. Across 37 mutually significant pathways, 59.5% were concordant between the iPSC model and human adipose tissue, including the pathways most central to FPLD2 pathophysiology: adipogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, and inflammatory response. These findings establish this isogenic iPSC system as a faithful cellular model of FPLD2 adipocyte biology and a platform for functional characterization of LMNA variants of uncertain significance.

papers.title: Recurrent mitotic error and purifying selection shape chromosomal mosaicism across human tissues
papers.abstract: Mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs) have been extensively studied in cancer and clonal hematopoiesis but less so in healthy solid tissues. Here, we characterized mCAs in 19 tissues across 25 donors (aged 42-89+ years) by analyzing >200x whole-genome sequencing data generated by the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network. Across 722 tissue samples, we identified 1,008 autosomal mCAs >1 Mb in length and ubiquitous losses of sex chromosomes. Surprisingly, the highest levels of Y chromosome loss in males (5-10% cell fraction in elderly donors) were observed in the lung, adrenal gland, and heart. These tissues also tended to experience more X loss in females, revealing a gradient of mitotic error burden across human tissues. Autosomal aneuploidies displayed distinct tissue-specific patterns indicative of negative selection against most events, except in the adrenal gland, in which low-level aneuploidy was pervasive. In contrast to the adrenal gland, testis rarely harbored aneuploidies but frequently experienced low-level copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH), suggesting increased mitotic recombination in spermatogonial stem cells. Recurrent X chromosome losses within tissues of female donors exhibited allelic skews explained by a combination of genetic and epigenetic effects. Together, these results show that the chromosomal landscape of aging human tissues is shaped by genetics and recurrent mutations, most but not all of which are held in check by purifying selection.

papers.title: Twenty-five new microsporidian genomes: Insights into ploidy, reproduction, and the group's pangenome
papers.abstract: Microsporidia are single-celled, obligately intracellular eukaryotic parasites of growing importance. Many aspects of their biology remain enigmatic, partly because of difficulties in sampling, culturing, and experimentally manipulating them. Here, we continue efforts to generate microsporidian genomes from serendipitously infected organisms sequenced for biodiversity genomics initiatives, such as the Darwin Tree of Life Project. We present 25 new microsporidian genomes: 14 biologically complete, including several at (near-)chromosome level, and 11 partial. Using RNA-seq data for three published genomes we identify Prokka as a suitable ab initio annotation approach for Microsporidia. Consistently annotating all available genomes, we investigate gene-content diversity across microsporidian clades. We find that the microsporidian pangenome exhibits extreme diversity, and that current genomic data substantially undersample the group's proteome space. Neither GC content nor genome span consistently explains orthogroup number across lineages, suggesting different evolutionary pressures. We find few one-to-one orthogroups in Microsporidia, as well as few orthogroups that are both lineage-specific and conserved across most species within a given lineage. Finally, Hi-C data confirm that tetraploid Amblyosporida microsporidia occur as two equivalent diploid units. In contrast, one Enterocytozoonida tetraploid genome suggests that all four genome copies occur within a single nucleus (a 'monokaryon'), confirming a previous proposal.

papers.title: Gene Embedding Hub: a standardized resource for human gene representations
papers.abstract: Gene embeddings are vector representations of gene identity that provide machine-learning models with information from diverse biological sources. However, their use is hindered by a lack of standardization: inconsistent identifiers, formats, and preprocessing conventions. In this work, we present a unified resource of 67 human gene-embedding sets derived from protein, DNA and RNA sequences, biomedical text, bulk expression data, single-cell expression models, functional data, biological networks, knowledge graphs, regulatory genomics and multimodal models, covering up to 20,097 GENCODE-annotated protein-coding genes. The collection includes both published precomputed embeddings and representations generated or extracted from publicly available models and biological data. Each embedding set is organized in a folder containing the embedding matrix, the Ensembl gene identifiers, machine-readable metadata, and processing documentation. We validate the resource by measuring global and local similarity, cross-embedding consensus, and cross-embedding predictability. The collection is designed to allow community-contributed embeddings that meet predefined technical and documentation requirements, enables comparison of gene representations across modalities and provides standardized embeddings for training and downstream applications.

papers.title: The Braarudosphaera bigelowii genome reveals cellular remodeling around a nitrogen-fixing organelle
papers.abstract: Braarudosphaera bigelowii hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial organelle UCYN-A, or the nitroplast, but the absence of a reference genome has limited investigation of the genomic features accompanying this association. Here, we present nuclear and organellar genome resources for the cultured B. bigelowii strain FR-21. The assembly comprises a 472.1-Mb nuclear genome together with representative nitroplast, chloroplast, and mitochondrial genomes of 1.49 Mb, 107 kb, and 44 kb, respectively. The four genomic compartments have strongly differentiated GC compositions, consistent with their distinct evolutionary origins. The large nuclear genome does not appear to reflect a corresponding expansion of protein-coding capacity. Repeat annotation indicates that approximately 77% of the nuclear assembly is repetitive, leaving approximately 108 Mb of nonrepetitive sequence containing roughly 16,000 predicted protein-coding genes. Phylogenomic analysis places B. bigelowii within the expected diversity of haptophytes, indicating that its unusual diazotrophic lifestyle is not associated with an anomalous phylogenetic position. Comparative analysis of nitrogen metabolism genes reveals extensive remodeling of host nitrogen acquisition and assimilation. B. bigelowii lacks major components required for nitrate and nitrite assimilation and has reduced capacity to use urea, cyanate, and several internally recycled nitrogen sources. In contrast, ammonium transport and the glutamine synthetase-glutamate synthase pathway are retained. This combination suggests reduced flexibility in nitrogen use and a host metabolism increasingly centered on ammonium supplied by the nitroplast. B. bigelowii also encodes an expanded set of flavodoxin and cryptochrome genes. Eleven of 14 flavodoxin candidates and 21 of 39 cryptochrome candidates contained motifs linked to nitroplast targeting. Together with previous evidence that some of these proteins are abundantly imported into the nitroplast, these expansions point to host-encoded roles in nitroplast redox metabolism and diel regulation. These genome resources establish a foundation for investigating nitroplast protein import, host-organelle metabolic integration, and the genomic consequences of acquiring an intracellular nitrogen-fixing compartment. They further show that the evolution of the B. bigelowii-UCYN-A relationship involved substantial remodeling of genome architecture and nitrogen metabolism in both partners.

papers.title: Dissecting functional elements in giant genomes using the first generation of high quality salamander assemblies
papers.abstract: Salamanders are an enduring and historically significant group that helped originate multiple scientific fields of study, including regeneration, cytogenetics, experimental embryology, cloning, evolutionary developmental biology and evolution of extreme genome size. We generated a high-quality, single haplotype assembly for the 32 Gb axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) genome using an F1 hybrid between axolotl and a divergent relative the tiger salamander (A. tigrinum). Using multi-genome alignments to other salamanders that meet VGP metrics, we leveraged strong conservation of karyotypic structure to identify >523,000 highly conserved non-coding elements within massively expanded intronic and intergenic regions, the vast majority of which are unique to the salamander lineage. Orthogonal measures of chromatin state and enhancer activity confirmed that many conserved elements correspond to cis-regulatory sequences and identified several thousand that are utilized during regeneration. The conserved elements identified here will enable robust functional genomic analyses of tissue regeneration and other traits that uniquely empower salamander models in biological research.

papers.title: Genomic Correlates of APOBEC-Associated Mutagenesis in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: APOBEC-associated mutagenesis is prominent in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but genomic features associated with its intertumoral variability remain incompletely characterized. We investigated genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis while accounting for the compositional structure of mutational signature data. Methods: Mutational signatures were analyzed in 552 ESCC tumors from eight countries. APOBEC-associated mutagenesis was quantified as SBS2 plus SBS13 using absolute mutation counts and proportional contributions. Associations with co-occurring mutational signatures, total SBS burden, recurrent driver-gene alterations, and country were evaluated using correlation, sensitivity, and multivariable analyses. Principal component and regression-model robustness were additionally assessed. Results: APOBEC burden varied markedly across tumors (median, 2,002 mutations; IQR, 987-4,346). Several associations observed using signature proportions were not maintained in absolute-count analyses: SBS1, SBS3, and SBS5 changed direction, indicating sensitivity to compositional representation. In contrast, SBS18 remained inversely associated with APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in all variable pairings examined: proportion versus proportion (Spearman rho = -0.527), APOBEC proportion versus SBS18 absolute count (r = -0.435), and absolute count versus absolute count (Pearson r = -0.319, P = 1.59 x 10^-14; Spearman rho = -0.317). These are distinct comparisons rather than discrepant estimates. Notably, this cohort-wide relationship was primarily characterized by higher APOBEC burden in SBS18-negative than SBS18-positive tumors rather than a continuous inverse relationship among SBS18-positive tumors. The multivariable model had an in-sample R^2 of 0.400 but lower and variable 10-fold cross-validated performance (mean R^2 = 0.273). Country added little explanatory information to this model (delta R^2 = 0.008; global P = 0.402). ZNF750-mutant tumors had higher APOBEC burden than wild-type tumors (BH-FDR q = 0.0032), although only 12 tumors carried ZNF750 alterations. Conclusion: Genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in ESCC are sensitive to the representation of mutational signature activity. SBS18 showed the most consistent inverse association, whereas the ZNF750 association warrants independent validation.

papers.title: Single-base mapping of m6A in lncRNAs reveals a distinct landscape linked to transposable elements and RNA processing
papers.abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal RNA modification with established roles in mRNA metabolism. Although m6A has been characterized in several well-known long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), its transcriptome-wide landscape and roles remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized the m6A landscape of lncRNAs at single-base resolution, identified m6A deposition-associated features, and investigated potential roles of m6A in lncRNA processing. Unlike in mRNAs, m6A sites are broadly distributed along lncRNAs. We further found that these differences in m6A patterns between lncRNAs and mRNAs may reflect contributions from transposable element-derived sequence to motif availability and local RNA structure, together with splicing-related constraints on m6A deposition near exon junctions. Additionally, m6A may be relevant to the regulation of lncRNA polyadenylation. Together, these findings define the single-base-resolution m6A landscape in lncRNAs, and connect lncRNA methylation to transposable elements, RNA structure, splicing, and polyadenylation. This study broadens our understanding of m6A in the lncRNA epitranscriptome.

papers.title: Dynamic evolution of diaphorin biosynthetic genes against a background of genome conservation in Profftella
papers.abstract: The Asian citrus psyllid Diaphorina citri (Insecta: Hemiptera), a major agricultural pest, harbors the unusual obligate bacterial symbiont "Candidatus Profftella armatura" (Profftella), which is intimately integrated with its host yet devotes a remarkably large proportion of its highly reduced genome to the production of diaphorin, a bioactive polyketide. To gain insight into the evolution of this distinctive symbiont, we determined the genomes of Profftella and the co-resident nutritional symbiont "Candidatus Carsonella ruddii" (Carsonella) from Diaphorina lycii and compared them with previously characterized counterparts from D. citri and D. cf. continua. The Profftella and Carsonella chromosomes from D. lycii were 471 and 174 kb, respectively, and Profftella harbored an 8-kb plasmid. Genome organization and gene content were highly conserved across the three lineages. The diaphorin biosynthetic system likewise retained its overall organization, consistent with an important role for diaphorin in the Diaphorina symbiotic system. Remarkably, however, pronounced lineage-specific structural variation was observed in diaphorin synthases DipP and DipT, encoded by two of the 20 diaphorin biosynthetic genes. These synthases contained three extensively amplified tandem arrays of acyl carrier protein (ACP) domains that carry growing polyketide intermediates, with up to seven copies compared with one or two at corresponding positions in the related pederin synthases. All three regions of tandem ACP repeats showed copy-number variation among the Profftella lineages. This variation indicates that ACP amplification remains evolutionarily dynamic despite the otherwise highly constrained symbiotic genome. Together, our findings show that even highly integrated obligate symbionts retain evolutionary flexibility in specialized functional systems.

papers.title: Silent travelers: the potential of migratory birds and their ticks to introduce emerging viruses into Switzerland
papers.abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Parvoviridae, dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks (Rhipicephalus turanicus) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.

papers.title: Multi-scale haplotype signatures distinguish among evolutionary processes
papers.abstract: Natural selection embeds distinct genomic signatures as populations adapt to environmental pressures. Machine learning approaches, particularly deep neural networks, have emerged as powerful tools to detect adaptive signatures from genomic data. While machine learning has dramatically improved our ability to extract these signals from sequence variation, distinguishing among multiple evolutionary processes remains challenging. We introduce SHADES, a deep learning framework that employs information about sequence differences and their frequencies at various spatial resolutions to capture evolutionary signatures at different genomic scales. We found that SHADES has the capacity to distinguish among neutrality, selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression and outperformed several contemporary methods evaluated for both classification accuracy and power. In addition, SHADES remained robust to a number of confounding factors, with only modest changes in classification performance. Furthermore, application of SHADES to empirical haplotypic variation from European humans recovered previously reported signals for selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression, while also identifying novel genes broadly involved in immune defense, inflammatory regulation, and epithelial barrier biology.
